description: We're a team interested in software, space engineering, and data visualization. For Lunar Landing Site Navigator, we want to build an interactive tool that uses real lunar terrain to compare landing sites near the Moon's south pole. Change the landing date and see how sunlight and direct line of sight to Earth change.
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a free, browser-based tool for comparing lunar south pole landing sites and dates by sunlight and direct-to-Earth line of sight. Pick a candidate site or custom coordinates and a date, and the app shows the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon, solar elevation, time to sunset and Earthset, and how these change over a lunar day or a year.

It addresses the challenge gap: Horizons, Quickmap and Moon Trek are powerful but slow for quick "what if we slip two weeks or move 2 km?" comparisons. Our tool combines JPL SPICE/DE440 ephemerides with measured NASA LOLA terrain (20–80 m near the pole) in one interface with 2D/3D views, timelines, side-by-side comparison, a search for the five best surface-stay windows of a year, and CSV export.

Sun and Earth directions match JPL Horizons within 0.0006° over 4,326 checks, and annual illumination agrees with published studies to within 0.03–2.72 percentage points. A hypothetical rover mode shows how moving shadows, slopes and battery limits constrain surface operations.

It is a research and education tool, not certified for real landing decisions.
details:
What it does

Lunar Landing Site Navigator helps mission planners, students and the public answer one question quickly: where and when on the lunar south pole can a surface mission get sunlight for power and a geometric line of sight to Earth for direct communication?

- Site and date selection: curated research sites near the south pole (Connecting Ridge, de Gerlache rim, Shackleton area and others) or custom coordinates; any date 2024–2036.

- Sun and Earth vs. the real horizon: horizon panorama built from measured LOLA terrain, with Sun and Earth discs, solar elevation, and time to sunset / Earthset.

- Comparison: side-by-side site cards and timelines show how small changes in place or date change power and communication windows.

- Best windows: searches a whole year for the five highest-scoring surface-stay windows using adjustable Sun / Earth / short-night weights, and ranks nearby terrain points for the selected dates.

- 3D terrain: measured global Moon plus detailed polar crops, with layers for illumination, Earth visibility, slope and published permanently shadowed regions.

- Rover mode (Drive): a hypothetical rover drives on real terrain; routes respect slope, moving shadows, battery and time, and show why some targets are unreachable.

- Export: scientific CSV of Sun/Earth geometry and visibility, plus a separate trip CSV.

How it works

Hourly Sun and Earth vectors in the lunar frame are precomputed from JPL NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440). Terrain horizons are traced from NASA LOLA digital elevation models out to 300 km, with no atmospheric refraction (the Moon has none). The horizon depends on local terrain and lunar curvature. Heavy calculations (illumination maps, window search, routing) run in Web Workers so the interface stays responsive. Data load progressively: overview first, then detailed sites and ephemeris years on demand.

Validation

- Sun/Earth directions vs. independent JPL Horizons tables: 4,326 hourly comparisons at 3 sites, maximum difference ≤0.0006° (target 0.1°).

- Annual illumination vs. published studies: Connecting Ridge 92.07% vs 92.3% (Gläser et al.); Shackleton points within +0.49 to +0.69 pp of Saha et al. 2023; up to 2.72 pp elsewhere (different periods and terrain releases).

- 22 automated tests, build and browser scenario checks run on every publish via GitHub Actions; input data are verified by SHA-256 checksums.

Example finding (2027, 2 m mast, 7-day stay)

At Connecting Ridge the best stay is 9–16 January 2027 with 100% Sun and 100% Earth visibility and no night. At de Gerlache rim the same week gives only 44% Sun with an 85-hour night, but its own best week (17–24 January) reaches 100% / 100%. Choosing the date matters as much as choosing the site.

Benefits and impact

When hardware delays or launch slips force a new date or site, teams can evaluate alternatives in minutes in one interface instead of combining several expert tools. It also works as an educational tool that makes the extreme polar lighting environment visible.

Tools and technologies

JavaScript (ES modules), WebGL, Web Workers, HTML/CSS, Vite; Python (NumPy, Pillow, Rasterio, SpiceyPy) for data preparation; Node.js tests and Playwright browser checks; GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages. Runs in any modern browser; no installation or login.

Creativity and factors we considered

Scientific honesty first: only measured terrain, no invented relief; every dataset is credited with provenance and checksums. Clearly stated limits: Earth visibility is geometry, not a radio link budget; permanent shadow is not proof of ice; 15° landing / 20° rover slopes and battery values are scenario assumptions, not NASA requirements; descent is an animation. Performance on modest hardware, mobile/touch layouts and a guided tour for non-specialists.

Source code (MIT): https://github.com/Dima000000/NASA-lunar-navigator

Not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA. Research and education only; not operational landing or navigation certification.
